questions.question: You need to query `WHERE 'urgent' = ANY(tags)` on a column of type `text[]`. Which index type should you use?
options: B-Tree
GIN
BRIN
Hash
questions.explanation: GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) is designed for composite values like arrays and JSONB, mapping each individual array element back to the rows that contain it. A B-Tree sorts the whole array as a single value and cannot see inside it, so it cannot accelerate a 'contains element' search.

questions.question: For a BRIN index to provide meaningful query pruning, what must be true about the indexed column's data?
options: The column must contain only integers
The data must be physically sorted or highly correlated with disk storage order
The table must have fewer than 1,000 rows
The column must have a UNIQUE constraint
questions.explanation: BRIN stores only a Min/Max summary per block of disk pages. If the data is naturally ordered (e.g., an auto-incrementing timestamp inserted in sequence), each block's Min/Max range is narrow and non-overlapping, so Postgres can skip whole blocks that fall outside a query's range. If the data is randomly distributed across blocks, every block's range covers nearly the full dataset, so BRIN can't rule out any block and provides no speedup.

questions.question: A table receives 10,000 inserts/second, each row carrying a 20-element tags array indexed with GIN. Why does this create more index write load than a single-column B-Tree on the same table?
options: GIN indexes are always slower regardless of data shape
GIN writes one inverted-index entry per array element, so 10,000 inserts/sec with 20 tags each produces roughly 200,000 entry writes/sec versus ~10,000 for a B-Tree
GIN indexes cannot accept concurrent writes at all
GIN requires a full table rewrite on every insert
questions.explanation: A B-Tree writes one index entry per row (one leaf update). GIN, however, decomposes each row's composite value into its individual keys and writes an entry per key - so a 20-tag array means 20 entry writes for a single row insert. This write amplification is the central trade-off of GIN: excellent read performance for 'contains' queries at the cost of significantly higher write overhead.

questions.question: What does setting `fastupdate = on` (the GIN default) actually do to mitigate write amplification?
options: It disables the index temporarily during bulk loads
It buffers new key entries in a small unordered pending list, merging them into the main GIN structure in batches instead of inserting each key individually
It converts the GIN index into a B-Tree automatically
It skips indexing rows with more than 10 array elements
questions.explanation: Fast Update appends new keys to a temporary 'pending list' rather than immediately inserting each one into the main tree structure. Periodically - or during VACUUM, or when the list fills - the pending list is merged into the index in one batch operation, which is far cheaper than thousands of individual tree insertions. The trade-off is that reads must also check the pending list, so a very large unmerged list can slightly slow queries until the next cleanup.

questions.question: Which index type is best suited for `WHERE booking_range && '[2024-01-01 10:00, 11:00)'` (range overlap queries)?
options: BRIN
Hash
GiST
B-Tree
questions.explanation: GiST (Generalized Search Tree) uses a hierarchy of bounding shapes to quickly discard ranges or geometric regions that cannot possibly overlap the query target, making it the standard choice for range-overlap queries and spatial data (PostGIS). B-Tree cannot evaluate the && (overlap) operator efficiently because it only understands strict ordering, not geometric or range containment.

questions.question: You suspect an index is bloated after years of updates and deletes. Which production-safe command rebuilds it without blocking reads and writes?
options: DROP INDEX then CREATE INDEX
REINDEX CONCURRENTLY
VACUUM FULL
ALTER INDEX REBUILD
questions.explanation: REINDEX CONCURRENTLY rebuilds the index from scratch in parallel with normal operation, avoiding the exclusive lock that a plain REINDEX (or a DROP+CREATE) would take. Dropping the index first would leave queries running without it (and unprotected) until the rebuild finishes, which is far riskier in production.

questions.question: A table has a `status` column where 95% of rows are 'inactive' and queries almost always filter `WHERE status = 'active'`. What index pattern minimizes size while still speeding up these queries?
options: A full B-Tree index on status covering all rows
A partial index: CREATE INDEX ... ON users(email) WHERE status = 'active'
A BRIN index on status
No index is possible on boolean-like columns
questions.explanation: A partial index only indexes rows matching the WHERE clause, so indexing just the 5% of 'active' rows produces a dramatically smaller, faster-to-maintain index than indexing the entire table - especially valuable for soft-delete or status-flag tables where queries consistently filter to one value.

questions.question: An overnight `CREATE INDEX` on a 500M-row table appears to have died mid-build. What is the correct diagnostic and recovery sequence?
options: Immediately re-run CREATE INDEX with the same name and ignore any errors
Check pg_stat_progress_create_index for an active build, check pg_index for an invalid leftover entry, drop it if invalid, then rebuild using CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
Restart the entire Postgres server to clear the lock
Run VACUUM FULL on the table to force the index to complete
questions.explanation: pg_stat_progress_create_index reveals whether a build is still active and how far it progressed. If the backend died, pg_index may show an invalid (indisvalid = false) leftover index that should be dropped before retrying. Rebuilding with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (rather than a plain CREATE INDEX) avoids taking an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock that would block all writes to the table for the multi-hour duration of indexing 500M rows.
